title: Which Passive-Aggressive Smart Home Routine Are You Secretly Running?
dek: Your kitchen cylinder knows you're mad, but it doesn't know how to communicate it properly.
author: dirk-hotfix

questions.q: How do you register your displeasure when someone leaves a pantry door ajar?

answers.a: I subtly lower the kitchen thermostat to 61 degrees until they shiver.
I tap the kitchen cylinder to play a 3-second audio file of a heavy exhale.
I engage the smart-lock on the fridge and set the pantry bulb to pulse yellow.
I draw a tiny geofence around their shoes and trap the robot vacuum there.

questions.q: Your roommate starts talking while you are listening to a podcast. What is your automated response?

answers.a: I ask the cylinder to play a single, low-frequency hum that disrupts conversation.
I lock the bluetooth speaker to my phone and pause the audio, blinking the status ring.
I route the robot vacuum to aggressively bump into their chair legs.
I drop the ambient room temperature by three degrees and let the lights fade.

questions.q: It is 11 PM and they haven't taken the recycling out. How do you express this?

answers.a: I set the hallway smart bulb to blink in a slow, anxious rhythm.
I order the vacuum to only clean the exact strip of floor they walked on.
I drop the thermostat to 58 degrees and turn off the water heater.
I play a 4-second clip of a clock ticking loudly through the kitchen orb.

questions.q: They come home 30 minutes late without texting. What is the entry protocol?

answers.a: The front door locks with a loud clack, but the deadbolt requires a 10-second apology voice command.
The robot vacuum immediately abandons its dock to block the mudroom.
The kitchen cylinder greets them by playing a low, disappointed sigh.
The hallway lights fade to 12% and the thermostat drops to 60 degrees.

questions.q: They are chewing ice too loudly. How do you retaliate via the smart home?

answers.a: I lower the lights to 4% and let the thermostat free-fall.
I tap the glass cylinder to emit a high-pitched, 2-second dog whistle tone.
I lock them out of the kitchen via the smart-door and flash the hallway strobe.
I program the vacuum to repeatedly ram the base of their stool.

questions.q: They used your expensive ceramic mug and left it in the sink. Your move?

answers.a: I command the cylinder to play a muffled, 3-second sound of someone weeping softly.
I lock the dishwasher and make the sink light blink red.
I route the robot vacuum to clean only the single drop of coffee they missed.
I drop the kitchen temperature to 59 degrees and dim the pendant lights.

r1.title: The 'Dimming The Hallway Lights To 4% When The Thermostat Drops' Protocol
r1.body: You don’t yell. You don’t argue. You just let the ambient temperature in the living room drop to a brisk 61 degrees while the overhead lights fade to a barely perceptible amber. When your roommate asks why it feels like a Victorian orphanage, you stare blankly at the kitchen cylinder and say, 'The house is just settling.' You are communicating your deep, unresolved resentment through HVAC adjustments and lumens. They will eventually put on a sweater, but they will never actually apologize for leaving the milk out.
r1.share: I don't yell. I just let the ambient temperature drop to 61 degrees until you shiver.

r2.title: The 'Playing A Single 3-Second Audio Clip Of A Deep Sigh' Protocol
r2.body: Verbal confrontation is for people who lack a premium smart speaker subscription. When someone interrupts you, you don’t raise your voice. You just tap the glass top of your kitchen cylinder and command it to play 'Track 4' from your 'Miscellaneous Sighs' playlist. It’s a low, breathy exhalation that lasts exactly three seconds, played at 80% volume. It’s just loud enough to be heard over the refrigerator hum, but quiet enough to plausibly deny. You are translating your resentment into acoustic pressure. They know you’re mad. They just don’t know how to prove it.
r2.share: I don't argue. I just tap the glass cylinder and play a 3-second audio file of a heavy exhale.

r3.title: The 'Locking The Front Door But Leaving The Kitchen Orb Blinking' Protocol
r3.body: You’ve realized that physical locks are inadequate for true emotional quarantine. When your partner comes home late without texting, you don’t change the deadbolt code. You just ensure the smart lock engages with a loud, authoritative clack, while simultaneously setting the hallway smart bulb to pulse in a slow, anxious yellow. It’s the digital equivalent of crossing your arms and staring at the wall. You are trapping them in a highly specific, illuminated purgatory. They will stand in the foyer for four minutes before you finally grant them access to the couch.
r3.share: I don't change the locks. I just make the hallway bulb pulse yellow until you apologize.

r4.title: The 'Setting The Robot Vacuum To Only Clean The One Crumb They Dropped' Protocol
r4.body: You believe in restorative justice, but only if it’s highly localized and deeply inconvenient. When they drop a single pretzel crumb on the rug, you don’t ask them to sweep. You open the cleaning app and draw a tiny, invisible geofence around the crumb. The robot whirs over, spends forty-five seconds aggressively bumping into the coffee table, and then returns to its dock. You’ve turned a minor mess into a three-hour psychological operation. They will eventually pick it up themselves, just to make the machine stop judging them.
r4.share: I don't ask you to sweep. I just geofence the robot vacuum around your single dropped crumb.
